candidates.rationale: Weakest component: the denominator range TS_MAX($high,21) - TS_MIN($low,21). It is a two-observation statistic, so the scale jumps discretely whenever one extreme day rolls out of the window; that staleness is the regime story behind the monotone fade (2000 +0.0250 to 2013 +0.0010) while the numerator stays informative. Replacing it with the summed daily range keeps the same channel-position idea on a smooth, 21-day-wide scale that no single gap day can set. Stays in the documented normaliser family (derived series, not a guarded mean of a raw field) and uses window 21 rather than the archive's TS_SUM($high-$low,10), so the only shared complete subtree is $high - $low (3 nodes).

Weakest component: the TS_SUM($return, 5) leg. It owns both defects - 4.3-day IC half-life and 0.204 daily turnover, the highest in the set - because a 5-day signed return sum is a short-horizon reversal that must be re-traded every week. Wrapping the return in ABS and lengthening to 21 turns it into a realized-dispersion leg: same skeleton, same fundamental term, but the leg now persists over weeks and should cut turnover several-fold. Working memory says directional return aggregates buy little while ABS-return aggregates at 21 cleared at fitness 2.25-4.11, so this is the documented form of the leg. Two edits: insert ABS, window 5 -> 21.

Weakest component: the leading CS_DEMEAN(CS_RANK($roe)) term. It is the piece carrying the 0.725 archive correlation and the single negative year (2003 -0.0057), and working memory records that this exact leading term is spent - it drew both a 5-node archive_subtree hit and a rho 0.901 correlation hit in one round. The corr leg is the healthy half (25.3-day half-life, 0.104 turnover), so it is left untouched. Swapping to a plain accrual-quality z-score keeps the fundamental-minus-microstructure skeleton but changes the accounting dimension, which memory says is the edit that actually decorrelates; $accrual_gap is also on the dense side of the coverage gate. Three edits: drop CS_DEMEAN, CS_RANK -> CS_ZSCORE, $roe -> $accrual_gap.

Weakest component: the leading CS_DEMEAN(CS_RANK($roe)) term. At |rho| 0.794 this factor is one point off the correlation gate, and the archive member it sits against is a $roe-minus-microstructure expression, so the profitability leg is what is duplicated, not the leverage ratchet or the 42-day corr (which give the 41-day half-life and 0.033 turnover worth keeping). Working memory flags this leading term as exhausted and records that CS_ZSCORE on $asset_turnover carried the 3.1-4.1 accepts. Turnover is also the accounting dimension least redundant with the leverage-change leg already present. Three edits: drop CS_DEMEAN, CS_RANK -> CS_ZSCORE, $roe -> $asset_turnover.

Weakest component: the volume leg $dollar_volume / ($open + 1e-8) at window 63. Working memory records this family as exhausted - raw $dollar_volume, /$open and /TS_MEAN($dollar_volume,63) all came back rho 0.961-0.977 against the same archive member - and the two that cleared did so by putting the volume leg through TS_DELTA(...,5) or TS_RANK(...,10) and shortening the correlation window to 21. That is exactly this edit: leg transform and window changed together, not the normaliser. TS_RANK also makes the leg stationary within stock, which removes the reason the raw-level ratio needed a normaliser at all, and drops $open so the factor falls to 4 fields and sheds part of the 0.200 complexity charge. Three edits.

Weakest component: the raw $volume leg. This is the least stable parent in the set (0.86, negative in 2003 and 2013) and the cause is that $volume enters as an untransformed level: its cross-era drift means the 21-day correlation is measuring different things in 2003 than in 2013, which is a regime problem rather than a decay problem. A 10-day time-series rank makes the leg stationary within stock, and widening the correlation to 42 days steadies the estimate and should pull turnover below the parent's 0.110. Memory says leg transform and window must move together, and that TS_RANK(...,10) is one of the two volume-leg transforms that has cleared. The archive members here use raw $volume at 21 and TS_DELTA($high-$low,5) at 21, so no complete 4-node subtree is shared beyond $high - $low.

candidates.rationale: Weakest component: the TS_DELTA($dollar_volume, 5) leg. A 5-day difference is a one-week event detector, which is why this factor has the 4.7-day IC half-life and the highest turnover of the corr family (0.122) while its 21-day sibling holds 18.2 days - it is being asked to predict far past the horizon it measures. Replacing the fast difference with a 21-day dispersion of dollar volume asks whether volume variability tracks range variability, a persistent stock characteristic rather than an event, and widening the correlation to 63 days matches the estimation horizon to the holding horizon. Memory: dispersion kernels produced everything above 1.9, and a window rescale alone would not have decorrelated - the transform changes too. Total lookback 84 days, inside the 126 budget.

Weakest component: the denominator TS_MEAN($open, 10) + 1e-8. It is a guarded mean of a raw field, the exact pattern working memory says to stop using (three archive_subtree rejects), and it is the piece pushing |rho| to 0.789 against an archive member that normalises the same range by TS_MEAN($open, 42). It also contributes nothing informative: dividing a 10-day range by a 10-day price mean makes a volatility ratio whose denominator is just a size proxy. Normalising by the same series over a longer window makes it self-normalising - a short-over-long range ratio, scale-free without borrowing a price level - and drops $open to 3 fields. Window 42 keeps it off the archive's TS_MEAN($high-$low,63) normaliser, so only $high - $low (3 nodes) is shared. Two edits.

Weakest component: the multiplier TS_MAX($high, 21) / ($open + 1e-8). It is a raw price-level ratio close to 1 for every name, so it scales the leverage-change leg by something with almost no cross-sectional information while spending the fifth field and the full 0.200 complexity charge; memory also records the high-over-TS_MAX chassis as saturated. Replacing it with 21-day realized volatility keeps the multiplicative skeleton but gives it a reason to exist: rising leverage is only a red flag on names whose returns are already volatile. Fields fall to 4, which lifts the complexity charge, and the parent's 0.017 turnover and 38-day half-life should be preserved since both legs stay slow. Three edits.

Weakest component: TS_RANK($close, 168). It is the binding constraint on coverage - 0.912 is the tightest margin in the set, and working memory records a 189-day price leg as the only outright coverage failure in a round, with 126 days the practical ceiling. It is also a raw $close kernel, the weakest cheap-screen bucket. Cutting to a 42-day window buys back roughly four months of history for every name, and switching the field to $dollar_volume keeps the product's second leg in the fundamental-rank-times-TS_RANK(volume) form that memory says carries the top fitnesses, with the fundamental leg CS_ZSCORE($accrual_gap) left intact so the product combinator still has its required fundamental side. Two edits.

prompt:
You are proposing quantitative factor expressions for US large-cap equities.

Universe and data
- S&P 500 point-in-time constituents, roughly 500 names per day.
- Daily bars only, plus point-in-time quarterly fundamentals stamped from the
  report date. Every field is referenced with a leading `$`:
    $open $high $low $close $adj_close $volume $dollar_volume $return
    $roa $roe $operating_margin $leverage $asset_turnover
    $book_per_share $earnings_per_share $accrual_gap
  A bare name such as `close` is not a field and will be rejected.
- Execution convention: the signal is computed after the close of day T and the
  position is entered at the open of T+1.
- The window these factors are fitted and judged on runs from 2000 to 2013.
  Do not reason about anything later; you will never be shown a number from
  outside that window.

Syntax
- Operators are function calls: TS_MEAN, TS_STD, TS_MAX, TS_MIN, TS_RANK,
  TS_DELTA, TS_CORR, TS_COV, TS_SUM, TS_PRODUCT, TS_ARGMAX, TS_ARGMIN,
  TS_DECAY_LINEAR, EMA, DELAY, DELTA, RANK, ZSCORE, CS_RANK, CS_ZSCORE,
  CS_DEMEAN, IF, IF_ELSE, MIN, MAX, ABS, SIGN, LOG, LN, SQRT, POWER, BOUND,
  COUNT.
- Lookback windows must be positive integer literals, e.g. TS_MEAN($close, 21).
- Guard every division with a small epsilon: `/ (TS_STD($close, 21) + 1e-8)`.
- Well-formed example: -RANK(TS_CORR(RANK($close), RANK($volume), 5))

Hard limits every proposal must satisfy, or it is rejected before it is scored
- at most 200 characters
- at most 5 distinct `$fields`
- at most 4 free numeric constants (lookback windows and
  the 1e-8 epsilon guard do not count)
- expression tree depth at most 6
- must not share a complete sub-expression of 4 or more
  nodes with any published Alpha101 formula, or with any factor already in the
  archive. Restating a published alpha is the one thing that is always rejected.
- must cover at least 90% of the panel
- absolute rank correlation below 0.80 against every archive member

Output
- Return valid JSON only, matching the supplied JSON schema. No prose outside it.


TASK: MUTATE. For each parent below, identify its single weakest component and
change ONLY that component.

A mutation is localized: the returned expression must be within
3 tree edits of its parent. Rewriting the idea is not a mutation
and will be rejected. Say which node you changed in `changed_node`, and put the
parent's id in `parent_ids`.

Read the diagnostics: a factor whose IC is positive in most years and negative in two has a regime problem, one with high turnover is paying costs it does not earn back, and one whose IC half-life is short is being asked to predict too far ahead. Change the component responsible for the specific weakness you name.
